books.description: Zheng He commanded fleets of up to 300 ships — including vessels four times the size of Columbus's Santa Maria — and sailed from China to Africa 70 years before Europeans reached the Indian Ocean. China then burned the records of his voyages and turned inward. 100 facts about the greatest naval expedition in history that the world almost forgot.

books.title: 100 Facts About John Franklin
books.subtitle: The Arctic Explorer Whose Disappearance Became a Global Mystery
books.description: John Franklin's 1845 Arctic expedition — 129 men and two ships — vanished completely. The search to find them launched over 40 expeditions, mapped more of the Canadian Arctic than any previous effort, and produced one of the greatest mysteries in exploration history. The wrecks of his ships were not found until 2014 and 2016. 100 facts about the disappearance that haunted Victorian England for 170 years.

books.title: 100 Facts About Alexander von Humboldt
books.subtitle: The Explorer Who Invented Modern Environmental Science
books.description: Humboldt climbed the highest mountain yet ascended by any human, mapped the magnetic equator, discovered the ocean current that bears his name, and was the first person to describe climate change caused by human activity — in 1800. Darwin called him the greatest scientific traveler who ever lived. 100 facts about the explorer who saw the Earth as a single connected living system two centuries before everyone else.

books.title: 100 Facts About Thor Heyerdahl
books.subtitle: The Man Who Crossed the Pacific on a Raft
books.description: Thor Heyerdahl sailed 4,300 miles from Peru to Polynesia on a balsa wood raft called the Kon-Tiki in 1947 to prove that ancient South Americans could have reached the Pacific Islands. The voyage took 101 days and he nearly died twice. His book about it became one of the bestselling nonfiction titles of the 20th century. 100 facts about the anthropologist who proved his theory by risking his life on a raft.

books.title: 100 Facts About Edmund Hillary
books.subtitle: The Mountaineer Who Reached the Roof of the World
books.description: Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reached the summit of Everest on May 29, 1953 — the news reached London the morning of Queen Elizabeth II's coronation. Hillary was a beekeeper from New Zealand who had no formal mountaineering training when he began climbing. 100 facts about the beekeeper who stood on top of the world.

books.title: 100 Facts About Bartolomeu Dias
books.subtitle: The Navigator Who First Rounded the Cape of Good Hope
books.description: Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1488 during a storm so violent he did not realize he had done it until the weather cleared and he found himself sailing northeast. He named it the Cape of Storms — the Portuguese king renamed it the Cape of Good Hope. 100 facts about the navigator who opened the sea route to Asia and never got credit for it.

books.title: 100 Facts About Leif Erikson
books.subtitle: The Viking Who Reached America 500 Years Before Columbus
books.description: Leif Erikson established a settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland around 1000 AD — 492 years before Columbus arrived in the Caribbean. The site was confirmed by archaeology in 1960 and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. 100 facts about the Viking explorer who reached America half a millennium before history gave anyone else the credit.

books.title: 100 Facts About Ponce de León
books.subtitle: The Explorer Who Searched for the Fountain of Youth
books.description: Ponce de Leon became the first European to set foot in what is now the United States when he landed in Florida in 1513 — and the Fountain of Youth story was probably invented by his enemies to mock him. He was killed by a poisoned arrow on his second expedition to Florida. 100 facts about the conquistador whose legend outlasted his actual extraordinary discoveries.

books.title: 100 Facts About Vasco Núñez de Balboa
books.subtitle: The First European to See the Pacific Ocean from the Americas
books.description: Balboa crossed the Isthmus of Panama in 1513, waded into the Pacific Ocean in full armor, and claimed the entire ocean and all lands touching it for the Spanish Crown — an act of territorial ambition so vast it defied comprehension. He was beheaded for treason four years later. 100 facts about the conquistador who claimed an entire ocean and paid for his ambition with his head.

books.title: 100 Facts About Meriwether Lewis
books.subtitle: The Explorer Who Mapped the American West for the First Time
books.description: Lewis and Clark's Corps of Discovery traveled 8,000 miles from St Louis to the Pacific Ocean and back in two years, catalogued 178 previously unknown plant species and 122 unknown animals, and lost only one man — to appendicitis on the second day. 100 facts about the expedition that revealed half a continent to the nation that had just bought it.

books.title: 100 Facts About James Clark Ross
books.subtitle: The Man Who Found the Magnetic North Pole
books.description: James Clark Ross located the Magnetic North Pole in 1831, later commanded the most successful Antarctic expedition of the 19th century, and discovered the Ross Sea, Ross Ice Shelf, and two volcanoes — one of which he named after his ship Erebus, the same ship that later vanished with Franklin. 100 facts about the polar explorer who mapped the ends of the Earth.

books.title: 100 Facts About Fridtjof Nansen
books.subtitle: The Norwegian Who Crossed Greenland and Reached the Farthest North
books.description: Nansen crossed the Greenland ice sheet on skis in 1888 — a feat no one had attempted — then deliberately froze his ship into Arctic pack ice to drift across the polar sea, reaching a new record for farthest north. He later won the Nobel Peace Prize for his work with refugees. 100 facts about the explorer who pushed farther north than any human before him and then dedicated his life to helping others.

books.title: 100 Facts About Jacques Cartier
books.subtitle: The French Navigator Who Claimed Canada for France
books.description: Jacques Cartier made three voyages to Canada, sailed up the St Lawrence River, and became the first European to reach the interior of North America — naming the country after a Huron word he misunderstood. He also brought back what he believed were gold and diamonds that turned out to be iron pyrite and quartz. 100 facts about the navigator who claimed Canada for France and came home with fool's gold.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Roman Empire
books.subtitle: The Empire That Built the Western World
books.description: At its peak the Roman Empire contained 70 million people — a quarter of the world's population — connected by 250,000 miles of roads, a single currency, and one legal system. Its roads, laws, language, and architecture still shape the world every person reading this lives in. 100 facts about the empire whose shadow never left us.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Mongol Empire
books.subtitle: The Largest Contiguous Empire in Human History
books.description: The Mongol Empire covered 24 million square kilometers — more than twice the size of the Roman Empire — and was built in less than 80 years by a people with no cities, no writing system, and no professional army before Genghis Khan. It connected Europe to China for the first time and the Black Death traveled its trade routes westward. 100 facts about the most explosive empire ever assembled.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Ottoman Empire
books.subtitle: The Empire That Ruled Three Continents for Six Centuries
books.description: The Ottoman Empire lasted 623 years — from 1299 to 1922 — spanning three continents, 29 conquered nations, and the reigns of 36 sultans. At its peak it controlled the eastern Mediterranean, North Africa, the Middle East, and southeastern Europe, and its collapse directly caused World War One. 100 facts about the empire whose end shaped the modern Middle East.

books.title: 100 Facts About The British Empire
books.subtitle: The Empire on Which the Sun Never Set
books.description: At its peak in 1922 the British Empire covered 24 percent of the Earth's land surface and contained 412 million people — one in four humans alive. It spread the English language, common law, and cricket to every continent and its borders, drawn with little regard for existing peoples, still cause conflicts today. 100 facts about the largest empire in human history and the world it left behind.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Persian Empire
books.subtitle: The First Superpower the Ancient World Ever Saw
books.description: The Achaemenid Persian Empire was the largest the ancient world had ever seen — stretching from Greece to India and containing 44 percent of the world's population at its peak. Cyrus the Great issued the world's first human rights declaration, allowing conquered peoples to keep their religions and customs. 100 facts about the empire that invented the idea of tolerance as a tool of power.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Byzantine Empire
books.subtitle: The Roman Empire That Survived a Thousand More Years
books.description: When the Western Roman Empire fell in 476 AD, its eastern half kept going for another 977 years — preserving Roman law, Greek philosophy, and Christian theology through the Dark Ages until Constantinople finally fell to the Ottomans in 1453. The Byzantines called themselves Romans until the very end. 100 facts about the empire that refused to accept Rome was finished.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Han Dynasty
books.subtitle: The Empire That Defined Chinese Civilization
books.description: The Han Dynasty ruled China for 400 years, invented paper, the seismograph, and the civil service exam, opened the Silk Road, and established a cultural identity so powerful that Chinese people still call themselves Han today. At its peak it was one of the two most powerful empires on Earth alongside Rome. 100 facts about the dynasty that gave China its enduring identity.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Aztec Empire
books.subtitle: The Warrior Empire That Fed Its Gods with Human Blood
books.description: The Aztec capital Tenochtitlan was built on an island in a lake, had a population of 200,000 — larger than any European city of its era — and a market that astonished the Spanish soldiers who saw it. The empire it controlled sacrificed thousands of people per year to keep the sun moving across the sky. 100 facts about one of history's most extraordinary and most brutal civilizations.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Inca Empire
books.subtitle: The Empire That Built Roads Across the Andes Without the Wheel
books.description: The Inca Empire built 25,000 miles of roads across the Andes Mountains without the wheel, the horse, or iron tools — using only human labor, bronze, and stone. Their postal relay system could send a message 1,500 miles in five days. The entire empire was destroyed in two years by 168 Spanish soldiers. 100 facts about the most remarkable engineering civilization the Americas ever produced.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Egyptian Empire
books.subtitle: The Civilization That Endured for Three Millennia
books.description: Ancient Egypt lasted 3,000 years — longer than the time between Cleopatra and today. When Cleopatra was born, the Great Pyramid of Giza was already 2,500 years old. The civilization produced 170 pharaohs, built monuments that still stand, and developed writing, medicine, and mathematics that influenced every culture that followed. 100 facts about the longest-lasting civilization in human history.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Arab Caliphates
books.subtitle: The Empires That Created the Islamic Golden Age
books.description: While Europe was in the Dark Ages, the Islamic Caliphates preserved Greek philosophy, invented algebra, developed optics, advanced astronomy, and created hospitals, universities, and public libraries. Baghdad's House of Wisdom was the greatest centre of learning in the world for 500 years. 100 facts about the empires that kept human knowledge alive when the Western world had forgotten it.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Mughal Empire
books.subtitle: The Dynasty That Built the Taj Mahal
books.description: At its peak the Mughal Empire produced 25 percent of global GDP — more than all of Western Europe combined. It gave the world the Taj Mahal, the concept of the rupee, and administrative systems that the British later copied when they took over. 100 facts about the empire that made India the wealthiest region on Earth.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Spanish Empire
books.subtitle: The First Empire to Span Both Hemispheres
books.description: The Spanish Empire was the first to span both hemispheres and the first on which the sun never set — a phrase used about Spain before it was ever used about Britain. At its peak it controlled 13 percent of the world's land surface and extracted so much silver from the Americas that it caused global inflation. 100 facts about the first truly global empire in human history.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Carthaginian Empire
books.subtitle: The Empire That Almost Destroyed Rome
books.description: Hannibal crossed the Alps with 37 war elephants, invaded Italy, won every major battle for 15 years, and killed 70,000 Romans at Cannae in a single afternoon — the worst defeat in Roman history. Rome eventually won by refusing to fight him and instead attacking Carthage directly. 100 facts about the empire that came closer than anyone to stopping Rome from conquering the world.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Holy Roman Empire
books.subtitle: Neither Holy Nor Roman Nor an Empire
books.description: The Holy Roman Empire lasted over a thousand years, covered most of central Europe, and was so politically fragmented that Voltaire said it was neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire. It contained over 300 separate states at its most chaotic and was held together primarily by the idea that it existed. 100 facts about the strangest political entity in European history.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Maurya Empire
books.subtitle: The First Empire to Unite the Indian Subcontinent
books.description: Chandragupta Maurya unified the Indian subcontinent for the first time in history, and his grandson Ashoka — after a battle so bloody it reportedly killed 100,000 people — converted to Buddhism, renounced violence, and issued the world's first animal welfare laws. 100 facts about the empire that produced both India's greatest conqueror and its most enlightened ruler.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Qin Dynasty
books.subtitle: The Dynasty That Unified China and Built the Great Wall
books.description: The Qin Dynasty lasted only 15 years but unified seven warring states, standardized weights, measures, currency, and writing across China, built the first Great Wall, and created the 8,000-strong Terracotta Army to guard its emperor in death. The name China itself comes from Qin. 100 facts about the shortest and most consequential dynasty in Chinese history.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Mali Empire
books.subtitle: Home to the Richest Man Who Ever Lived
books.description: Mansa Musa of Mali is estimated to have been worth 400 billion dollars in today's money — more than Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, and Bill Gates combined. When he made his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 with 60,000 attendants and 12 tons of gold, he gave away so much that he crashed the Egyptian economy for a decade. 100 facts about the wealthiest empire and the richest individual in human history.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Khmer Empire
books.subtitle: The Empire That Built the World's Largest Religious Monument
books.description: The Khmer Empire built Angkor Wat — the largest religious monument ever constructed — as well as a hydraulic system that supported a city of one million people in the middle of a jungle. At its peak Angkor was the largest pre-industrial city on Earth. 100 facts about the empire hidden by the jungle for 500 years and still not fully understood.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Napoleonic Empire
books.subtitle: The Empire Napoleon Built and Lost
books.description: In 15 years Napoleon built an empire covering most of Europe, introduced the Napoleonic Code that still forms the basis of law in 70 countries, and then lost everything in Russia when his 600,000-man army was reduced to 100,000 by winter and disease. He was exiled twice and died on a remote island. 100 facts about the empire that remade Europe and vanished almost as fast as it appeared.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Russian Empire
books.subtitle: The Empire That Stretched Across Eleven Time Zones
books.description: The Russian Empire was the third largest empire in history, covering 22 million square kilometers across eleven time zones — when it was noon in St Petersburg it was already the next day in Vladivostok. It expanded by an average of 55 square miles per day for 300 years. 100 facts about the empire that grew continuously for three centuries and collapsed in a week.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Ming Dynasty
books.subtitle: The Empire That Built the Forbidden City
books.description: The Ming Dynasty built the Forbidden City with one million workers and 100,000 artisans, completed the Grand Canal, constructed the final and most famous version of the Great Wall, and sent the largest fleet in history to explore the Indian Ocean — then turned inward and closed China to the world. 100 facts about the dynasty that built China's most enduring monuments and then chose isolation.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Japanese Empire
books.subtitle: The Empire That Modernized in a Generation
books.description: In 1853 Japan had no railways, no telegraphs, and a feudal military armed with swords. By 1905 it had defeated Russia — a European great power — in a full-scale naval war. The speed of Japan's industrial and military transformation remains one of the most remarkable national reinventions in history. 100 facts about the empire that went from samurai to superpower in fifty years.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Assyrian Empire
books.subtitle: The World's First Military Superpower
books.description: The Assyrians created the world's first professional standing army, the first iron weapons used in warfare, the first siege engines, and the first organized system of psychological terror as a military strategy — relocating entire conquered populations to break their will to resist. They were feared across the ancient world for 300 years. 100 facts about the empire that invented the template for military dominance.

books.title: 100 Facts About The Austro-Hungarian Empire
books.subtitle: The Empire at the Center of World War One
books.description: The Austro-Hungarian Empire contained 11 official languages, 15 major ethnic groups, and no shared national identity — held together by a Habsburg emperor and the bureaucracy he ran. The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo triggered a war that killed 20 million people and erased four empires from the map. 100 facts about the empire whose collapse remade the modern world.
